title: The Attention Economy
description: A podcast episode about how apps compete for our time, what the research says and who should be responsible for fixing it.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Welcome to the attention economy
parts.intro: You will hear the hosts of a podcast, Linh and Nam, introducing the topic of the attention economy.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Welcome back to Deep Focus, the show about how we spend the one thing we can't make more of. I'm Linh.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: And I'm Nam. Today, the attention economy. And I'll confess something: I checked my phone four times while preparing this episode's notes.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Only four? I'm impressed. The phrase attention economy, for listeners new to it, goes back to an economist who observed in the nineteen-seventies that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. When information is abundant, what becomes scarce is the capacity to process it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Which flips the old model. For centuries the scarce thing was content. A book was expensive, a newspaper was a daily event. Now the content is effectively free and endless, so the contest is over who gets our minutes.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: And that is where the business model comes in. If you're not paying for a service, you're not exactly the customer. Advertisers pay, and what they buy is your time in front of the screen. So platforms are rewarded for any design that increases it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I want to be careful here, because I find that line a bit glib. It implies we're passive victims. Plenty of people use these apps deliberately and benefit enormously.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Fair. I'd say it's less a conspiracy than an incentive. Nobody sits in a dark room plotting to ruin your evening. They simply measure what keeps you scrolling, and then they do more of it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's a distinction worth making. The harm, if there is any, comes from optimisation without anyone asking whether it's good for you.

parts.title: Part 2 · How apps hold our attention
parts.intro: You will hear Nam interviewing Dr Cole, who studies the design of apps.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Dr Cole, you've studied the design of apps for years. What's the technique people talk about most?

script.speaker: Dr Cole
script.text: The infinite scroll, probably, though I'd argue it's less sinister than it sounds. It removes a stopping cue. In a book, a chapter ends, and the end gives you a natural moment to ask whether you want to continue. A feed never ends, so the question never arises.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: So it's not that it's addictive, it's that it takes away the pause.

script.speaker: Dr Cole
script.text: Precisely. I'm wary of the word addiction. Clinically it means something specific, and most people's habits don't meet that definition. But a habit can be a problem without being an addiction.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: What about the little red dot, the notification?

script.speaker: Dr Cole
script.text: That works through unpredictability. Psychologists found long ago that rewards arriving at irregular intervals produce the most persistent behaviour. Sometimes your phone offers something delightful, sometimes nothing. Never knowing which keeps you checking. Slot machines run on the same principle.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: That's slightly alarming.

script.speaker: Dr Cole
script.text: It should be a little alarming, but I'd stress that the same principle powers perfectly harmless things, like fishing, or opening the post. The question is not whether a mechanism exists but whether it's used in your interest.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: And is there evidence that all this harms us?

script.speaker: Dr Cole
script.text: The honest answer is mixed. Large studies find small average effects on wellbeing. But averages hide a lot: for some adolescents, particularly those already struggling, the effects look considerably bigger. I'd say the evidence justifies caution, rather than panic.

parts.title: Part 3 · A week with a plain phone
parts.intro: You will hear Linh describing an experiment she tried for the podcast.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Now for the segment where one of us tries something foolish so you don't have to. This week I spent seven days with a plain phone: no feeds, no news apps, only calls, messages and maps.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: The first two days were, frankly, uncomfortable. I kept reaching for my pocket the way you keep touching the gap where a tooth used to be. On the second afternoon, queueing at a bakery, I realised I had no idea what to do with my hands, my eyes or, worse, my thoughts.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Then something odd happened. By day four, the queue had become interesting. I noticed the baker's habit of humming, and an old man who was teaching his grandson to count coins. I'd walked past that bakery for years without seeing it.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I should be honest about the downsides. I missed a friend's invitation because it came through an app I'd removed, and I arrived at a meeting having not read an article everyone else had read. I felt, for about an hour, slightly left out. Which tells you something about how much of my sense of being informed was really a fear of missing out.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: My conclusion isn't that technology is the enemy. I returned to my usual phone on day eight, and, to be candid, within a week I was back to old patterns. What changed is that I now notice the pull. I ask myself, do I want this or has it just been placed in front of me?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: My producer, who is far more disciplined than I am, says that's the whole secret. She keeps her phone in a drawer in another room and says the trick is making the good thing easy and the bad thing slightly annoying.

parts.title: Part 4 · Who should fix it?
parts.intro: You will hear Linh and Nam answering a listener question about regulation.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Let's turn to the listener question that arrived most this week. Should governments regulate this, or is it a matter of personal responsibility?

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: I'd say personal responsibility is the answer people give when they don't want to think about the structure. It's rather like telling people to choose healthier food in a street full of vending machines.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I'm sympathetic, but I'm wary of rules. Regulators are slow, and technology changes every few months. A law written for today's feeds could be obsolete by the time it takes effect.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That's an argument for writing principles rather than technical rules. Some places are already requiring that children's accounts have limits by default, and that people can easily turn off personalised recommendations.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Defaults, yes. That I like. Most of us never change a setting, so whoever chooses the default chooses the behaviour of millions.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Which is exactly why default settings are the most powerful design decision in the industry, and the least discussed. If a platform started every account with notifications off, I suspect the whole conversation would change within a year.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Then perhaps the thing to ask is not how to make people stronger but how to make the environment kinder.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Though I'd hate us to sound as if individuals have no part. We can still choose to be bored occasionally.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Boredom, the last luxury. On that note, thank you for listening. Try leaving your phone in another room tonight, and tell us what you notice.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: And if you can't bear it, tell us that too. We won't judge. After all, Nam checked his four times.

questions.text: What did the economist observe about information?
options: Plenty of information leads to a shortage of attention
Information is only valuable when it is expensive
Information becomes cheaper as attention becomes cheaper
Attention grows as more information is produced
questions.explanation: Linh explains that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention, because processing capacity becomes scarce.

evidence.quote: a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention

questions.text: How has the scarce resource changed over time, according to Nam?
options: From advertising revenue to free content
From daily news to weekly podcasts and magazines
From newspapers to books and libraries
From content to people's time and attention
questions.explanation: He says content used to be scarce but is now free and endless, so the contest is over who gets our minutes.

evidence.quote: so the contest is over who gets our minutes

questions.text: What is Nam's attitude to the idea that users are not the customer?
options: He believes it is the most important point about the industry
He thinks it is too simple because it makes users passive
He thinks it applies only to children using free apps
He is convinced that advertisers are secretly plotting against users
questions.explanation: He calls the line a bit glib and says it implies people are passive victims, when many use apps deliberately.

evidence.quote: I find that line a bit glib

questions.text: Why does Nam say he checked his phone four times?
options: To prove that apps are addictive for most people
To criticise the producers of the programme for overworking him
To admit humorously that the topic applies to him
To explain why he is late for the show
questions.explanation: It is a light confession at the start, showing that even the host is affected by the subject.

evidence.quote: I checked my phone four times while preparing this episode's notes

questions.text: What does Linh suggest about the cause of any harm?
options: It comes from incentives, not from a deliberate plan
It comes from laws that are too strict for platforms
It comes from users who lack enough self-control
It comes from a deliberate plot by advertisers
questions.explanation: She says it is less a conspiracy than an incentive, because companies simply measure what keeps people scrolling.

evidence.quote: it's less a conspiracy than an incentive

questions.text: According to Dr Cole, why is the infinite scroll effective?
options: It removes a natural point to stop
It shows more advertisements than other designs
It rewards users with points
It makes content load faster
questions.explanation: She says it removes a stopping cue, so the question of whether to continue never arises.

evidence.quote: It removes a stopping cue.

questions.text: What is Dr Cole's attitude to the word addiction?
options: She thinks it is a harmless exaggeration in most cases
She is cautious because it has a specific clinical meaning
She uses it freely to describe all heavy phone use
She believes that it only applies to teenagers and young adults
questions.explanation: She says she is wary of it because clinically it means something specific that most people's habits do not meet.

evidence.quote: I'm wary of the word addiction

questions.text: Why do notifications keep people checking their phones?
options: They always contain good news
They are impossible to switch off
They are louder than other sounds
The rewards are unpredictable
questions.explanation: She explains that rewards arriving at irregular intervals produce the most persistent behaviour, as with slot machines.

evidence.quote: Never knowing which keeps you checking.

questions.text: Why does Dr Cole mention fishing and opening the post?
options: To suggest that people prefer old habits to new ones
To prove that slot machines are perfectly safe to use
To show that the mechanism itself is not harmful
To compare apps with other traditional hobbies and pastimes
questions.explanation: She says the same principle powers harmless activities, so what matters is whether it is used in your interest.

evidence.quote: The question is not whether a mechanism exists but whether it's used in your interest.

questions.text: How does Dr Cole view the evidence on harm?
options: She thinks it proves that apps do serious damage to everyone
She thinks it calls for caution rather than panic
She thinks it shows that there is no real problem at all
She thinks it is too weak to be worth discussing
questions.explanation: She says the evidence is mixed with small average effects, but larger for some adolescents, so it justifies caution.

evidence.quote: the evidence justifies caution, rather than panic

questions.text: How did Linh feel during the first two days of the experiment?
options: Angry and anxious about missing the news
Curious about the people queueing at the bakery
Uncomfortable and unsure what to do with herself
Relieved and calm to be free of her phone
questions.explanation: She calls the first two days uncomfortable and says she did not know what to do with her hands, eyes or thoughts.

evidence.quote: The first two days were, frankly, uncomfortable.

questions.text: What does the bakery story suggest about Linh's normal habits?
options: She rarely went out in the afternoons at all
She preferred to queue in silence with her thoughts
She disliked the baker's humming and the long queues
She had stopped noticing her surroundings when waiting
questions.explanation: By day four she noticed details she had missed for years, implying her phone had been absorbing her attention.

evidence.quote: I'd walked past that bakery for years without seeing it.

questions.text: What does Linh conclude from feeling left out at the meeting?
options: Her friends should have contacted her in a different way
Feeling informed partly came from a fear of missing out
She needed to read more articles before every meeting
News apps are essential for anyone working in an office
questions.explanation: She says the feeling tells her how much of her sense of being informed was really a fear of missing out.

evidence.quote: a fear of missing out

questions.text: What is Linh's main conclusion about the experiment?
options: The experiment changed none of her thinking or habits
The main gain was noticing the pull, not giving up technology
She would keep the plain phone permanently after all
Technology is the real enemy of human attention
questions.explanation: She says technology is not the enemy and that she went back to old patterns, but now notices the pull.

evidence.quote: What changed is that I now notice the pull.

questions.text: Why does Linh mention her producer?
options: To explain why she missed the invitation to the party
To suggest that producers are better at discipline than hosts
To offer a practical tip: change the environment, not yourself
To complain about the difficulty of working with a producer
questions.explanation: The producer keeps her phone in a drawer in another room, making the good thing easy and the bad thing slightly annoying.

evidence.quote: making the good thing easy and the bad thing slightly annoying

questions.text: What is Linh's view of the personal responsibility argument?
options: It is correct for adults but not children
It ignores the way the environment is structured
It is the only realistic solution
It is too expensive to put into practice
questions.explanation: She compares it to telling people to eat healthily in a street full of vending machines.

evidence.quote: personal responsibility is the answer people give when they don't want to think about the structure

questions.text: What is Nam's main worry about regulation?
options: Laws may be out of date before they take effect
Rules would make apps more expensive for ordinary users
Governments do not understand how children use apps
Regulators are too strict with technology companies
questions.explanation: He says regulators are slow, and technology changes quickly, so a law could be obsolete when it begins.

evidence.quote: A law written for today's feeds could be obsolete by the time it takes effect.

questions.text: Why does Linh talk about principles and default settings?
options: To answer Nam's objection that rules become outdated
To praise the work of regulators
To argue that children should not use apps
To show that technical rules are better
questions.explanation: She replies that writing principles rather than technical rules avoids the problem, and gives examples of default limits.

evidence.quote: That's an argument for writing principles rather than technical rules.

questions.text: Why are default settings so powerful, according to Nam?
options: Most people never change them
They are cheaper to design
They are chosen by users themselves
They are hidden from regulators
questions.explanation: He says most of us never change a setting, so whoever chooses the default shapes the behaviour of millions.

evidence.quote: Most of us never change a setting

questions.text: What do the speakers agree on by the end?
options: Governments alone can solve the problem of attention online
The environment matters, but individuals still play a part
Technology companies should be closed down within the year
Individuals should take all of the responsibility themselves
questions.explanation: Nam suggests making the environment kinder, and Linh adds that individuals have a part, for example by choosing to be bored.

evidence.quote: We can still choose to be bored occasionally.
